UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                     )
PJM Interconnection, LLC                             )              Docket No. ER26-3515
                                                     )

     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF PENNSYLVANIA
       GOVERNOR JOSH SHAPIRO IN SUPPORT OF PJM’S PROPOSAL TO
     ESTABLISH INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE AND A LARGE
                          LOAD REGISTRY

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro (Governor

Shapiro) respectfully submits this motion for leave to answer and answer in support of PJM

Interconnection, LLC’s (PJM) proposal pursuant to Federal Power Act (FPA) Section 205 to

establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) and a Large Load Registry. The

Commission should grant leave to answer to clarify certain issues and assist the Commission

with its decision-making.

I.     SUMMARY

       PJM faces a crisis: large load growth has overwhelmed the region’s ability to serve that

new demand in a reliable manner, driving skyrocketing costs and increasing the risk of reliability

events, which may require manual load shed to protect the bulk power system.2 In that serious

demand . . . has grown despite a net increase of 1,294.4 MW of Installed Capacity . . . the
addition of new supply has not kept pace with rapid large load demand growth”); Opening
remarks of Chair Swett, AD26-7 Transcript at 9 (July 23, 2026) (“PJM is the tip of the spear, it's
the laboratory of national and economic security on which our country may rise or fall”);
Opening remarks of Deputy Sec. of Energy Danly, AD26-7 Transcript at 32-34 (“PJM is a mess .

                                                1
 context, IRAS is a critical measure to protect the region’s reliability and its ratepayers, consistent

with the Governors’ and the Administration’s Statement of Principles3 and the Ratepayer

Protection Pledge.4 The central thesis for those documents was that the data centers that are

predominantly causing the present reliability crisis and spurring the need for new energy

infrastructure should bear its costs. Pennsylvania is doing its part to meet the moment, advancing

solutions to the current crisis within the Commonwealth—as described by the Pennsylvania

Public Utility Commission in its filing in this docket—but no state can address the looming

reliability emergency singlehandedly. PJM’s proposed mandatory, region-wide pre-emergency

IRAS program is a necessary short-term fix to protect Pennsylvania residents and business—as

well as PJM customers broadly—from the unjust and unreasonable harm of resource adequacy

shortfall and related power outages.

        Opponents raise three principal objections to PJM’s proposal, none of which warrant its

rejection.5

        First, protestors are wrong that PJM has veered beyond its jurisdiction. PJM is squarely in

its lane to operate the bulk power system in order to maintain system reliability including, where




Council Lake, AD26-7 Transcript at 45-46 (“PJM is clearly broken, multiple failed capacity
markets, capacity auctions, sky high price increases.”).

principles-regarding-pjm.

secures-american-ai-dominance-protects-consumers/.

  The Governor Shapiro focuses on challenges to the core design features of IRAS raised in the
protests of the Data Coalition Center (DCC); Google; Vistra; Talen; Constellation; EPSA; and
P3. Filers raise a host of other, less central, objections to IRAS. Because PJM has consented to
modifications of its proposal consistent with NRG, if the Commission finds any validity to such
objections, it may direct PJM to file tariff modifications sufficient to address them.

                                                  2
 necessary, directing the curtailment of load. Under its proposal, PJM properly leaves the task to

the retail authority to determine which individual retail customers face disruption of service due

to changes in system-level operation. PJM has also appropriately provided solicitude to the states

by granting retail authorities a direct role in determining whether to provide wholesale

compensation based on the curtailments directed under IRAS and, if so, how much compensation

up to the cap proposed by PJM.

       Second, opponents incorrectly argue that IRAS unduly discriminates against new large

loads6 and/or existing generators.7 The new large computational loads that are causing the

current strain on the region’s infrastructure are not similarly situated to other loads due to their

unique features. Their addition is not organic load growth that might cause the need for rapid

system expansion and new supply in the ordinary course. It is a new and distinct threat to

reliability and affordability in the region. Treating these new loads as distinct matches reality.

Likewise, it is not discriminatory to recognize the difference between a capacity resource that is

already committed to serve system needs and a resource that has not yet assumed such a

commitment. To the contrary, it is common sense to distinguish between new capacity that is

available to serve new large loads, and existing capacity that is not. This is wholly consistent

with designing a reliability construct that directs curtailment signals to zones/areas hosting new

large loads that have not secured sufficient new capacity to meet their needs.

       Third, protestors’ remaining arguments are largely contradictory, revealing the weakness

of those objections. For example, some argue that IRAS will not be effective in incenting new

large loads to bring their own capacity because only retail authorities, not PJM, decide which

11.
7
  Constellation Protest at 37-40; Vistra Protest at 12-14.

                                                  3
 specific retail customers are allocated a share of zonal load curtailment8 but at the same time

insist IRAS is too stringent, will disrupt expectations, and new large loads need a longer

transition period to be just and reasonable.9 Both allegations cannot be true.

        Rather, IRAS is just and reasonable because it will increase the incentive for new large

loads to invest in new capacity in order to decrease the likelihood that they face curtailment of

their operations. IRAS is also just and reasonable because a given zone only faces the planning

horizon risk of pre-emergency curtailment proportionate to the share of new large loads that fail

to meet their own need for supply, which the zone has allowed to interconnect. The aspect of

curtailment that PJM controls, i.e., operation of the bulk power system and aggregate MW

limitations on service imposed at the zonal transmission system-level, is appropriate and

commensurate with the risks posed to the bulk power system. PJM is not responsible for, and

IRAS cannot be deemed unjust and unreasonable due to, actions (i.e., allocation of zonal

curtailment to individual customers) that later may occur through the independent decision of a

state retail authority.

        Protestors also object to removal of new large loads that do not Bring Your Own New

Capacity (BYONC) from the VRR Curve10; but that treatment is precisely the actual result of

implementing IRAS. In periods of capacity shortage when IRAS is in effect, new large loads will

not be served by system resources during periods of system strain. It is just and reasonable to

isolate demand that is not being served by system capacity from being reflected in the demand

curve. Exclusion of such load is necessary to accurately reflect the needs that are expected to be




8
  Google Protest at 3 (“IRAS will not incentivize new large loads to bring their own capacity”).
9
  DCC Protest at 35 (requesting, if it does not reject IRAS, that the Commission direct PJM to
include a “meaningful transition” that limits application of IRAS).
10
   Google Protest at 23-24.

 served by system resources, and to protect existing customers from costs that they did not

contribute to. Likewise, objections to PJM’s proposed order of curtailment are policy judgments

that do not render the design unjust and unreasonable. Rather, PJM’s design of IRAS to curtail

zones/areas with large load growth not matched by new supply before calling on demand

response products is an appropriate choice to protect existing customers because flipping that

order would reduce available capacity to meet regional needs by deterring demand response

registration.

          In addition to their legal flaws, many of these protests fly in the face of commitments the

same protestors already made in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and are essentially an

argument that the new capacity needed to serve data centers must be paid for by all PJM

customers through higher capacity market prices rather than by the actual cost-causers. IRAS is

both just and reasonable and critical to vindicate the shared commitment in the Governors’ and

the Administration’s Statement of Principles to “allocate costs to data centers . . . to load serving

entities with new data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be

curtailable.”

          PJM’s proposal of IRAS is necessary and appropriate in response to the severe challenges

facing the region. Protestors’ intimations that PJM ignored better alternatives such as a state-led

curtailment regime is legally irrelevant, but also incorrect.11 PJM’s decision to implement a

mandatory, pre-emergency, region-wide solution is necessary leadership and serves to protect

customers in response to requests from many state entities for such a uniform regional approach.

States can, of course, independently implement actions within their jurisdictional authority to

mitigate the challenges of large load growth, but they face the risk that such actions are not



11
     DCC Protest at 2-4; Google Protest at 23-25.

                                                    5
 compatible with or recognized under PJM’s tariff, or that other states fail to take commensurate

action.12 Failure to implement a consistent approach throughout the region could lead to a

patchwork strategy that could frustrate PJM’s real-time operations and fail to achieve the goals of

the implementing states.13 Given the urgency of this situation, only coordinated, region-wide

action like IRAS can mitigate the severe cost and reliability challenges caused by large load

growth imminently exceeding available supply. Governor Shapiro therefore urges the

Commission to approve IRAS without delay, as timely implementation is critical to have IRAS

in effect in time to avoid disruption of service for existing customers and to ensure its rate-

protective effects are in place before the next Base Residual Auction in December.




12

load connection queue process standards Dominion asserted that it could not consider the
impacts of load flexibility to reduce impacts on the transmission system or resource adequacy in
load interconnection studies because of PJM system planning requirements. Dominion asserted

non-firm or flexible load in both planning studies and system operations.” Similarly, Dominion
asserted that “implementation of any fast-track or accelerated connection mechanism” for
flexible loads “requires PJM rulemaking and FERC guidance.” Dominion, Rebuttal Testimony of
Jacqueline R. Vitiello, Exhibit No. 25, VA SCC Case No. PUR-2026-00011, at 15-17 (filed Apr.

Rebuttal Testimony of R. Matthew Gardner, Exhibit No. 21, VA SCC Case No. PUR-2026-
00011, at 7-8 (filed Apr. 30, 2026),
https://www.scc.virginia.gov/docketsearch/DOCS/8c2j01!.PDF (“the Company needs FERC and
PJM to take action on developing a formal framework for non-firm or flexible load planning and
establish rules around a customer bringing its own new generation before the Company can
begin to implement that framework.”). Dominion thus articulated the case for a coherent federal
regulatory approach as proposed by PJM in IRAS. State regulators face barriers to know when
the potential for inconsistency with a federal jurisdictional scheme genuinely warrant delay, or
when such concerns lack merit and are raised to delay costly or burdensome reforms.
13
   For example, PJM’s capacity shortage emergency procedures in Manual 13 for manual load
dumps after EEA3 generally assign load shed requests to deficient zones. However, if the PJM
Mid-Atlantic Region (MAAC) is deficient, the load shed is further allocated by the load shed
allocation table in Attachment E. As such, a state within MAAC could implement a voluntary
state IRAS program, and zones within that state could still face emergency EEA3 curtailments
based on actions of other states and zones within MAAC.

 II.    ANSWER IN SUPPORT OF IRAS

      A.     IRAS properly targets wholesale sales and reliable operation of the bulk
power system.

       Protestors variously characterize IRAS as “aim[ing] to interrupt retail service”;

“compel[ing] states . . . to conform their retail curtailment frameworks to PJM tariff

requirements”;14 “target[ing] retail customers . . . by mak[ing] the characteristics of the retail

customer . . . the basis for a curtailment obligation”15; and failing to “directly affect wholesale

rates.”16 None of these descriptions match the basic facts of PJM’s proposal. As PJM explains

IRAS is a “supplemental capacity product” that may be called upon during “an Interim Resource

Adequacy Service Action,” an action PJM anticipates will occur when it “is no longer able to

maintain reserves within the RTO or zone” or “there are insufficient resources to keep

[Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits] within defined operating limits in order to prevent

instability, uncontrolled separation, or cascading outages that adversely impact the reliability of

the interconnection.”17 PJM’s proposal is manifestly aimed at provision of a wholesale product or

service, and at ensuring reliable operation of the bulk power system; each is clearly within its

jurisdiction. Indeed, actions that would be possible under IRAS are no different from other

actions (or “Operating Instructions,” as defined by NERC) that PJM has long been authorized to

take as the region’s Reliability Coordinator, Transmission Operator, and Balancing Authority.18

The Operating Agreement already expressly grants PJM the authority to coordinate curtailment

curtailed in a zone or area and the Transmission Owner or Electric Distributor determines the

and reasonable and neither of which matters for PJM’s jurisdiction: (1) the implementation of

curtailment signals prior to an EEA 1, and (2) the means by which PJM will determine the

aggregate MW of load reduction directed within a zone or area. Implementing IRAS on a pre-

emergency basis prior to a NERC EEA 1 will avoid escalating emergency procedures that

include but are not limited to shortage pricing and public calls for conservation, which would

represent socialization of costs, both financial and reliability related, being imposed by non-

capacity backed new large loads upon all customers. For target MW reductions, PJM proposes to

limit the total MWs of load reduction in a zone or area based on the share of new large loads

(which PJM terms “Eligible New Large Loads”) that have failed to meet their capacity needs

through BYONC or capacity procured pursuant to Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP)

rules.20 However, PJM does not direct the curtailment of these loads, rather it uses these criteria

to set the aggregate MW reduction amount. It remains up to the retail authority to work with

entities within their jurisdiction to implement the retail end-user curtailment priority. PJM’s

focus on non-capacity backed new large loads to determine the MW reduction target in each

zone or area is appropriate, since these entities are precipitating the reliability emergency. Duly

targeting load reductions in zones or areas with non-capacity backed new large loads as a means

to potentially avoid emergency procedures is a just and reasonable method for avoiding unjust

customers who have paid for the embedded costs of the existing system and have not contributed

to the resource adequacy shortfall. Furthermore, the focus on zones or areas projected to have

capacity shortfalls in real-time—through the existence of non-capacity backed large loads in the

planning horizon—is consistent with PJM’s Operating Agreement Schedule 1, Section 1.7.11

which states that in an emergency “the Office of the Interconnection may not order a manual

load dump in a Control Zone solely to address capacity deficiencies in another Control Zone.”21

In other words, PJM is appropriately aligning IRAS with existing practices that generally limit

curtailment signals to zones with real-time capacity shortfalls.

       In short, PJM is asserting no new novel authority in proposing IRAS, but rather is

enhancing its deployment of existing tools to better ensure bulk system reliability (directing

loadshed to areas with concentrations of non-capacity backed new large loads) and equitable

wholesale market rates (more fairly allocating the risk of curtailment to zones or areas of the grid

that have most contributed to the problem).

       Protestors acknowledge that PJM does not propose to direct the curtailment of any

specific retail customer.22 In fact, PJM’s inability (and its disavowal of any attempt to do so) to

control the curtailment priority among individual retail customers is simultaneously a point of

contention for protestors.23 But protestors cannot logically claim both that PJM’s proposal

guarantee which individual retail customers are curtailed. Both cannot be true.

       Stripped of embellishment, the facts are straightforward: under IRAS, PJM can only

direct “a MW quantity of load reduction to the relevant Electric Distributer zone(s)/area(s)”24—it

neither targets nor directs specific retail customers to be subject to curtailment, nor compels or

restricts the authority of the retail authority to prioritize among the retail customers that must be

curtailed in order to meet the required MW quantity of bulk load reduction and safeguard the

reliability of the grid. This is what PJM and other balancing authorities have long existed to do.

       Protestors also make much of the fact that PJM’s determination of the MW quantity of

bulk load reduction is based upon the characteristics of retail customers in the relevant Electric

Distributer’s zone or area—i.e., that PJM proposes to base its curtailment of wholesale customers

on whether the load growth in that zone or area is comprised of new Large Loads (i.e., a large

and concentrated addition of 50 MW or more at the same electrical location) and whether such

new Large Load additions have been matched by addition of commensurate new supply (new

capacity in the form of BYONC or allocated RBP resources).

       Protestors’ position appears to be that PJM must blind itself—that it is legally barred

from acting on information about the characteristics of load growth in a zone or area, even if that

information is directly relevant to reliable operation of the bulk power system and enables PJM

to provide a just and reasonable wholesale product or service. There is no merit to this position.




assurance that new large loads will receive the purported benefit of BYONC because it is up to
states and EDCs to decide curtailment orders and priorities”).
24
   PJM Transmittal at 86.

        The caselaw on jurisdiction under the FPA has never drawn such rigid and restrictive

boundaries on the information that is plainly relevant to setting a wholesale rate.25 The

characteristics of retail loads and generation, both matters that reflect state regulation, are highly

relevant and essential to inform a wholesale rate. Taking this information into account in

designing the wholesale rate does not constitute regulation of those matters. It rather merely

constitutes prudent regulation of wholesale rates in light of the “fact . . . that the wholesale and

retail markets in electricity, as in every other known product, are not hermetically sealed from

each other.”26

       If adopted by the Commission, the protestors’ position would bar PJM from taking into

consideration information about generating facilities—ramp rates, minimum run times, outage

rates, and so on—because neither the Commission nor PJM have authority to directly regulate

generation. This jurisdictional rule would be absurd and unworkable if applied to generating

facilities in the context of running a wholesale energy or capacity market, and it is equally so if

applied to retail loads. PJM is not barred from seeking information about the nature of the load

growth in a zone, even if those matters are subject to retail jurisdiction, and using that

information to shape wholesale market rates.

be a clear division between areas of state and federal authority).
26

        B.      PJM’s proposed compensation framework provides appropriate solicitude to
       the states and is jurisdictionally sound.

       Protestors separately challenge PJM’s provision of an opportunity for wholesale

compensation for loads that provide IRAS as prescribing a retail rate.27 A number of state

regulators who have not otherwise challenged IRAS raise questions and concerns about the

proposed compensation structure, and some request that PJM or the Commission clarify that the

wholesale compensation proposal is not aimed at or a limitation on state authority to regulate the

retail rate.28 While Governor Shapiro is sympathetic to states’ requests to clarify these

provisions, so clarified, the proposal is jurisdictionally sound. Rather than target or set retail

rates, PJM’s proposal appropriately recognizes the states’ interests and affords states a unique,

but not unprecedented, role in implementing the wholesale market rate. Under established

Commission precedent upheld by the Supreme Court, availability of a wholesale rate may

depend on retail conditions, as PJM proposes here.

       Governor Shapiro understands the confusion that has resulted from PJM’s provision of

wholesale compensation for a wholesale service because it envisions making that wholesale

compensation level subject to change by the relevant retail authority. Providing such solicitude

to the state regulatory authority to exert circumscribed authority over aspects of a wholesale rate

has precedent, in the context of matters like wholesale demand response and wholesale

participation of distributed energy resources where both federal jurisdiction and state jurisdiction

exist over the same nexus of activities (e.g., a demand reduction can be sold as part of a



27
   DCC Protest at 12 (“PJM’s tariff revisions seek to prescribe the amount paid to retail
customers through their retail rates for service interruptions implemented at PJM’s direction”).
28
   See e.g., Comments, Request for Clarification, and, in the alternative, Request to Sever of
OPSI (“OPSI Comment”) at 8 (generally supporting key design elements of IRAS but requesting

Large Loads that determine the compensation level or retail regulators).

                                                  12

in Order No. 719, in solicitude to the states’ retail authority over retail customers, the

Commission granted the relevant electric retail regulatory authority (RERRA) a veto over that

existence of the wholesale transaction entirely. 29 Accordingly, the Commission required

RTO/ISOs to amend their market rules to permit demand response aggregators to bid in demand

response into wholesale markets, unless the RERRA’s laws or regulations do not permit such

participation.30 To this day, Order No. 719’s provision for a state opt-out limits demand response

participation in wholesale markets.

        Here, PJM has proposed an even more circumscribed role for the retail regulatory

authority over the wholesale rate than that provided by the Commission under Order No. 719.

Whereas under Order No. 719, a retail authority has a dispositive role in determining whether the

wholesale transaction may occur at all, PJM proposes in IRAS only to allow retail authority to

determine, from a range of just and reasonable compensation levels, which just and reasonable

compensation level to select. Specifically, by proposing a wholesale market compensation rate

from zero dollars up to a cap of 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate, PJM is setting a

default wholesale rate of 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate that will, absent other action

by the retail authority, pass through to retail rates. Only if the retail authority acts to change that

default rate to another just and reasonable compensation level, including potentially to zero,

would that alternative wholesale compensation level apply and flow through to retail rates.31 As

in Order No. 719, providing such a role for the retail authority does not render the wholesale rate

30

remains at the wholesale level and the state role would be authorized and defined in a federal

wholesale rate is setting conditions under which that rate applies (i.e., absent state action, rate x

applies; under conditions of state action y, rate z applies).

       PJM’s transmittal and proposed tariff revision arguably could be clearer in describing the

respective jurisdictional roles of PJM, as the public utility subject to federal jurisdiction that has

power to propose a change to wholesale rates, and the retail authority, which has no authority to

change that wholesale rate once it is established, but has authority pursuant to state law to

determine how to allocate that charge among retail customers. At times, PJM confusingly

appears to be speaking about compensation that would be provided to individual retail

customers, which can only be provided via retail, not wholesale bills.32 But PJM is also clear that

curtailment during an IRAS event is directed only as a MW quantity of load curtailment, i.e.,

bulk load, to a particular Electric Distributer’s zone or area,33 and wholesale compensation will

therefore accrue (presumably as a credit) on a wholesale bill to the wholesale customers based on

that total MW quantity of load curtailment. PJM acknowledges repeatedly in its filing that which

individual retail customers receive that compensation is beyond its control.34 Cleaning up PJM’s

“Eligible New Large Loads,” entities that PJM will not directly interface with in implementing

the wholesale rate, would helpfully clarify that PJM is setting a wholesale rate (in which retail

authority is permitted a role in implementation) rather than dictating terms of compensation to

specific retail customers. Similarly, PJM’s proposed tariff would benefit from clarification to

specify that provision of particular levels of compensation depend on certain conditions at retail.

In other words, just as eligibility to participate as wholesale demand response depends on

permission under the relevant state laws and regulations, wholesale compensation for IRAS at a

reduced level depends on RERRA action specifying such an alternate compensation level within

the acceptable, just and reasonable range. Such a reformulation would clarify that the retail

authority is not setting the wholesale rate, but rather that conditions in the retail context inform

the implementation of and are an input into the wholesale rate. Given PJM’s agreement to

alterations of its proposal consistent with NRG, we understand such clarifications of PJM’s

compensation structure to be permissible as they leave intact PJM’s core rate design (the

wholesale curtailments remain subject to wholesale compensation within the same just and

reasonable range as the initial proposal).

       C.      IRAS is not unduly discriminatory.

       Protestors contend that IRAS is unduly discriminatory in its treatment of new large loads,

existing capacity resources, or both.36 But it is not unduly discriminatory to distinguish between

                   2.     It is not undue discrimination to treat capacity resources that are

          Protestors’ argument that PJM’s proposal unduly discriminates against existing capacity

resources is also meritless. IRAS seeks to mitigate unique impacts to the grid from rapid

additions of very large quantities of load in a single electrical location without commensurate

addition of capacity. For that purpose, existing capacity resources, which cannot serve those new

large loads because they are already committed to provide capacity to the system, and new

capacity (including new capacity that is created at existing generating facilities or at deactivated

generating facilities), which is capable of serving the needs of new large loads and therefore can

reduce the transmission system impacts of such additions, must be distinguished. The question is

not whether resources that qualify new large loads to avoid curtailment under the IRAS scheme

(as BYONC or via allocated RBP UCAP) and existing capacity resources are capable of

providing the same “capacity, energy, and ancillary services products” in PJM’s wholesale

markets.44 Rather the question is whether existing capacity resources can solve the specific and

unique operational challenges caused by large load additions that PJM aims to solve with IRAS.

The unqualified and commonsense answer is no. Resources that are already being counted upon

to meet existing system needs do not have the same ability to address new large loads’

incremental capacity needs.

          Allowing existing resources to meet the needs of new large loads—as BYONC or RBP—

would only be allowing for a rent-seeking shell game, as new large loads would seek out

available capacity resources made cheaper by years of ratepayer compensation, and existing

capacity resources would seek to lock-in long-term contracts with new large loads. This would
